    About student loans

    Student loans usually have stages: studying, a grace period after you finish, then regular repayments. The structured calculator models each stage as a row, so you can match your own loan.

    What it is

    A loan for tuition, books and living costs while you study. Repayment often doesn’t start until after you graduate or leave your course, usually following a grace period of a few months.

    Interest while you study

    • On many loans, interest keeps building up while you study and is added to the balance when repayment starts. Use Grace period rows for this.
    • Some loans let you pay just the interest while studying. Use Interest only rows.
    • If no interest is charged while you study, enter only the repayment rows with the amount you’ll owe at graduation.

    Repaying it

    • Standard plans spread repayment over about 10 years in equal monthly payments, modelled here with Calculated rows.
    • Paying the interest while you study stops the balance from growing.
    • Some government loans offer repayment based on income. That isn’t modelled here.

    Payment structure

    Add a row for each stage of the plan. Rows run in order, one after another, starting from the first payment month.

    Fixed amountA payment the client has agreed to, such as a down payment, a seasonal payment or a final balloon.
    Interest onlyPays just the interest for the month, so the balance stays the same.

    What is a structured loan?

    A structured loan has a repayment plan shaped around the borrower’s cash flow instead of one equal payment every month. Farmers may pay mostly after harvest, a new business may need a grace period before trading starts, and a vehicle or equipment buyer may prefer lower monthly payments with a larger final balloon.

    How the calculated installment works

    Interest is charged each month on the balance still owed. Fixed, interest-only and grace months are applied as you set them, and every row marked Calculated shares one base installment (scaled by its multiplier). That base installment is solved so the balance reaches exactly zero with the last payment.

    Common questions

    Why does the balance go up during a grace period?

    When nothing is paid, that month’s interest is added to the loan. You then pay interest on the higher balance, which is why grace periods raise the total cost.

    Can I leave out Calculated rows?

    Yes. If every row is a fixed amount, the calculator shows whether the plan leaves money owing or overpays at the end, so you can adjust the amounts.

    Is this how my lender will calculate it?

    It uses the standard reducing-balance method with monthly interest. Lenders may add fees, use daily interest or round differently, so check the final schedule in your loan offer.

    Fixed or variable: which could cost less?

    The same loan under each rate option, using your fixed offer and variable outlook. The orange bars show what happens if variable rates end up 2% higher than you expect.

    Why choose fixed

    • Your payment is certain, which makes budgeting easy.
    • You’re protected if market rates rise.
    • Often starts higher than variable, and leaving early can mean break fees.

    Why choose variable

    • Often starts lower than a fixed rate.
    • You benefit straight away when rates fall.
    • Usually more flexible for extra payments or early repayment.
    • Payments can jump if rates rise.

    Why combine both

    • Lock in certainty for the first years, when budgets are usually tightest.
    • Keep the flexibility and possible savings of variable later on.
    • Spreads your interest-rate risk instead of betting on one direction.
    • Common worldwide, such as 5-year fixed deals or 5/1 adjustable-rate mortgages.

    How a mortgage payment is worked out

    The loan amount is the property price minus your down payment. Each month you pay interest on the balance still owed, and the rest of the payment reduces the balance. With a fixed rate the payment stays the same. With a variable rate, the payment is recalculated whenever the rate changes, so the loan is still repaid by the end of the term.

    Fixed, variable, or both?

    A fixed rate gives certainty, a variable rate gives flexibility and the chance of paying less, and a fixed period followed by variable gives some of each. Nobody knows where rates will go, so the most useful question is how much a rise would hurt. The comparison above shows each option under your outlook and under a 2% rise, so you can choose the level of risk you’re comfortable with.

    Common questions

    How much down payment do I need?

    It depends on the lender and the country. A larger down payment lowers the loan amount, the monthly payment and the total interest, and may get you a better rate.

    Why include property tax and insurance?

    They’re part of the real monthly cost of owning a home, and in some countries lenders collect them with the mortgage payment. Adding them shows what you’ll actually pay each month.

    What happens to my payment when a fixed period ends?

    The loan switches to the variable rate at that time and the payment is recalculated over the remaining term. If rates have risen, the payment goes up. Many borrowers refinance or fix again before the period ends.

    Is this exactly what my lender will charge?

    It’s a close estimate. Lenders may add fees, use different rounding, or adjust variable rates on their own schedule. Check the figures in your loan offer.

    Shorten the loan or lower the EMI?

    The same prepayments, applied two ways. Shortening the loan usually saves more interest, while lowering the EMI frees up monthly cash.

    How prepaying changes your loan

    Why prepaying saves so much

    Interest is charged on the balance you still owe. Every extra payment goes straight to the principal, so every later month is charged less interest. That’s why prepayments made early in the loan save far more than the same amount paid near the end.

    Shorten the loan or lower the EMI?

    Keeping the same EMI and shortening the loan gives the biggest interest saving, because the higher payment keeps reducing the balance quickly. Lowering the EMI saves less, but gives you more breathing room each month. Many people shorten the loan when their budget is comfortable, and lower the EMI when cash is tight.

    Common questions

    Is prepaying better than investing the money?

    Prepaying gives a guaranteed return equal to your loan’s interest rate. If you can’t reliably earn more than that after tax, prepaying is usually the better choice. Keep an emergency fund before prepaying.

    Do lenders charge for prepaying?

    Some do, especially on fixed-rate loans. Enter the fee as a percentage of each prepayment to see your net saving after the fee.

    Does the lender apply prepayments the same way?

    Most apply them to the principal, but some ask whether you want a shorter term or a lower EMI. Check with your lender before you pay.

    Payoff order

      Avalanche vs snowball

      Both plans pay the same amount each month. They only differ in which debt gets the extra money first.

      Avalanche: highest rate first

      • Pay the minimum on everything, and put all extra money on the debt with the highest interest rate.
      • Saves the most interest and is usually the fastest.
      • The first debt can take longer to clear if it has a large balance.

      Snowball: smallest balance first

      • Pay the minimum on everything, and put all extra money on the smallest balance.
      • Clears debts sooner, and each quick win builds motivation.
      • Usually costs a little more interest than avalanche.

      Either way: roll it over

      • When a debt is paid off, its minimum payment rolls into the next one, so your payments “snowball”.
      • Keep your total monthly payment the same until you’re debt-free.
      • The best plan is the one you’ll stick with.

      How your total debt falls

      Bars show what you pay each year. The line shows your total debt still owed.

      How the calculator works

      Each month, interest is added to every debt and the minimum payment is made on each one. Whatever is left of your monthly budget goes to one target debt: the highest interest rate for avalanche, or the smallest balance for snowball. When a debt is cleared, its payment moves to the next target, so your total monthly payment stays the same until everything is paid.

      Which method should I choose?

      If saving money matters most, choose avalanche. If you need early wins to stay motivated, choose snowball. When your debts have similar rates, the two plans cost almost the same, so snowball’s quick wins can be worth it.

      Common questions

      What if I only pay the minimums?

      Minimum payments on credit cards are set to keep you paying for a long time. The comparison shows how long it would take and how much interest you’d pay, and warns you if a minimum payment doesn’t even cover the interest.

      Should I include my mortgage?

      Usually not. Mortgages have low rates and long terms. Most people focus on credit cards, personal loans and car loans first.

      Is this exact?

      It’s a close estimate using monthly interest. Card issuers may calculate interest daily, change minimum payments as your balance falls, or add fees.

      Why credit card debt takes so long to clear

      Credit cards charge high interest, and the minimum payment is usually a small percentage of your balance. As the balance falls, the minimum falls too, so more of each payment goes to interest and the debt drags on for years. Paying a fixed amount every month, even slightly above the first minimum, clears the card far faster.

      Tips to pay off a card faster

      Stop adding new spending to the card while you pay it down, pay a fixed amount instead of the minimum, and put any extra money on the card with the highest rate first. A 0% balance transfer can help too, but check the transfer fee and what the rate becomes after the offer ends. If you have several cards and loans, try the debt payoff calculator to compare the avalanche and snowball methods.

      Common questions

      How is the minimum payment worked out?

      It varies by card. Common rules are a percentage of the balance (often 1% to 3%), or the month’s interest plus 1% of the balance, with a fixed minimum such as 25. Check your statement and set the rule above to match.

      Why does new spending matter?

      Anything you add to the card each month has to be paid off too, so it slows down your progress. If your payment doesn’t cover the interest plus new spending, the balance never goes down.

      Is this exact?

      It’s a close estimate using monthly interest. Card issuers often calculate interest daily and may charge fees, so your statements could differ slightly.

      Cost of borrowing

      Interest plus fees for each offer. The loan amount is the same, so this is what really differs.

      Interest Fees

      What the numbers say

      Look at the total cost

      • The lowest monthly payment is often the most expensive loan, because a longer term means more months of interest.
      • Compare interest plus all fees.

      Use the APR

      • The APR includes fees, so offers with different fees can be compared fairly.
      • A low rate with high fees can have a higher APR than a slightly higher rate with no fees.

      Check the fine print

      • Ask about early repayment charges, late fees and whether the rate is fixed.
      • Make sure the monthly payment fits your budget comfortably.

      Balance over time

      How quickly each offer is paid down.

      Year by year

      What you pay each year with each offer, and what you still owe at the end of the year.

      How offers are compared

      For each offer, the monthly payment is worked out from the rate and term. The cost of borrowing is all the interest plus upfront fees and any monthly account fees. The APR is the yearly rate that makes the payments you make equal to the money you actually receive after upfront fees, so it puts every offer on the same footing.

      Common questions

      Should I always pick the lowest APR?

      The lowest APR is usually the cheapest for the same term. If terms differ, also check the total cost and whether the monthly payment fits your budget.

      What if the fees are added to the loan?

      Set that offer’s “Fees paid” to “Added to the loan”. The fees are then borrowed too, so you pay interest on them, and the comparison includes that cost.

      What goes into a car loan

      The amount you borrow starts with the vehicle price, minus any rebates, plus sales tax and fees if you add them to the loan. Your down payment and the equity in your trade-in reduce it. If you still owe more on your trade-in than it’s worth, that difference is added to the new loan.

      How long should a car loan be?

      Shorter terms cost less and help you build equity faster. Longer terms, like 72 or 84 months, lower the payment but cost more interest and can leave you owing more than the car is worth for years. That matters if the car is written off or you want to sell it early. A common guideline is to keep the car payment within about 10 to 15% of your take-home pay.

      Common questions

      What is a balloon payment?

      Some car finance plans leave a larger final payment at the end, which lowers the monthly payments. You can pay it, refinance it, or in some plans return the car instead. You pay interest on the balloon amount for the whole term.

      How fast do cars lose value?

      It varies by make, model and market, but new cars often lose a large share of their value in the first few years. Change the yearly rate to match the car you’re looking at.

      Is sales tax always reduced by a trade-in?

      No. It depends on where you live, so untick the option if your area taxes the full price.

      Lease or buy?

      The total you pay out, minus what the asset is worth to you at the end. Buying uses a loan with the same rate, term and down payment.

      Why lease

      • Lower monthly payments than buying the same asset with a loan.
      • Drive a newer car more often, or keep equipment up to date.
      • Businesses may be able to treat rentals as an expense. Check with your accountant.

      Why buy

      • You own it outright once the loan is paid.
      • No mileage limits or wear-and-tear charges.
      • Usually cheaper if you keep the asset for many years.

      Watch out for

      • Mileage limits and excess-wear charges on car leases.
      • Early termination fees if you end the lease early.
      • Whether rentals are in advance, which raises the effective rate.

      How the lease is paid down

      Bars show the capital and finance charges in each year’s rentals. The line shows the amount still outstanding, which ends at the residual value.

      CapitalFinance chargesOutstanding

      Rental schedule

      Select a year to see every rental.

      YearRental incl. taxCapitalFinance chargeTaxOutstanding

      Car lease vs finance lease

      With a car lease (an operating lease), you pay for the part of the car’s value you use during the term, plus a finance charge. The residual value is what the car is expected to be worth at the end, and you can return the car or buy it for that amount. With a finance lease, the rentals pay off the asset over the term, often with a small final payment, and you own it at the end.

      How car lease payments are worked out

      The monthly payment has two parts: depreciation, which is the price minus the residual value spread over the term, and a rent charge, which is the price plus the residual value multiplied by the money factor. The money factor is the interest rate divided by 2,400. Tax is then added to each payment where it applies.

      Common questions

      What is a good residual value?

      A higher residual value means lower payments, because you pay for less of the car’s value. It’s set by the leasing company based on how well the model holds its value.

      Why do rentals in advance cost more?

      Paying at the start of each month means the first rental is due straight away, so the money you effectively borrow is smaller for the same rentals, which makes the effective rate higher.

      Is this exact?

      It’s a close estimate. Leasing companies may add document fees, acquisition fees or charges for extra mileage, so check the figures in your agreement.

      When refinancing pays off

      Your running gain from refinancing: payments saved plus the difference in what you owe, minus the costs. It turns green at break-even.

      Everything you’d pay from today on each loan.

      YearCurrent: paidCurrent: owedNew: paidNew: owedRunning gain

      When does refinancing make sense?

      Refinancing usually pays off when the new rate is meaningfully lower, you plan to keep the loan past the break-even point, and the costs are reasonable. A lower payment alone isn’t enough: stretching the loan over a longer term can lower the payment but increase the total interest you pay.

      How break-even is worked out

      Each month, the calculator adds up the payments you save and the difference between what you’d owe on each loan, then subtracts the refinancing costs. Break-even is the first month this running gain is above zero. If you sell or repay before then, refinancing would have cost you money.

      Common questions

      Should I add the costs to the new loan?

      It means less cash upfront, but you borrow more and pay interest on the costs. The calculator includes that in the comparison.

      What about a cash-out refinance?

      Taking extra cash out increases the new loan. This calculator compares a like-for-like refinance of what you owe today.

      What is compound interest?

      Compound interest is interest earned on your original money and on the interest it has already earned. Each period, the interest is added to your balance, so the next period’s interest is a little bigger. Over long periods this snowball effect can make interest a larger part of your balance than the money you put in.

      The formula

      A = P × (1 + r/n)n×t A is the final amount, P the starting amount, r the yearly rate, n the number of times interest is compounded each year, and t the number of years. Regular contributions each grow the same way from the date they’re added.

      The Rule of 72

      A quick way to estimate how long it takes money to double: divide 72 by the yearly rate. At 6%, money doubles in about 12 years. At 9%, in about 8 years.

      Common questions

      What rate should I use for investments?

      Savings accounts and deposits have a stated rate. For investments like shares or funds, returns go up and down, so use a conservative long-term average and remember that past returns don’t guarantee future ones.

      What does “in today’s money” mean?

      Prices usually rise over time, so the same amount buys less in the future. Entering an inflation rate shows what your future balance would be worth in today’s prices.

      Does this include tax or fees?

      No. Interest and investment returns may be taxed, and funds may charge fees, both of which reduce growth. You can lower the rate to allow for them.

      What is a SIP?

      A Systematic Investment Plan means investing a fixed amount at regular intervals, usually monthly, into a mutual fund or similar investment. Because you invest every month regardless of prices, you buy more units when prices are low and fewer when they’re high, which is known as rupee-cost or pound-cost averaging.

      How the estimate works

      FV = P × [((1 + i)n − 1) ÷ i] × (1 + i)P is the monthly investment, i the monthly rate (yearly return ÷ 12), and n the number of months. Each SIP is assumed to be invested at the start of the month.
      Are SIP returns guaranteed?

      No. Market-linked investments go up and down. The expected return is an assumption, so try a few different rates to see a range of outcomes.

      What is a step-up SIP?

      A step-up SIP increases your monthly investment by a set percentage every year, for example 10%, so your investing keeps pace with your income.

      What is a lump sum investment?

      A lump sum investment puts a single amount of money to work at once, such as a bonus, an inheritance or the proceeds of a sale. Because all of it is invested from day one, it has the most time to compound.

      FV = P × (1 + r/n)n×tP is the amount invested, r the yearly return, n how many times a year returns are compounded, and t the number of years.
      Is a lump sum better than a SIP?

      If returns are steady, investing earlier earns more. But markets go up and down, so spreading your investment reduces the risk of investing everything just before a fall. Many people split the difference.

      How fixed deposit interest works

      A fixed deposit locks your money for a set tenure at a fixed rate. With the cumulative option, interest is added to the deposit each period and earns interest itself, so you receive everything at maturity. With a payout option, interest is paid to you monthly or quarterly and the deposit stays the same.

      A = P × (1 + r/n)n×tP is the deposit, r the yearly rate, n the number of compounding periods a year (4 for quarterly), and t the tenure in years.
      Which compounding is most common?

      Many banks compound fixed deposits quarterly. Check your bank’s terms, as more frequent compounding gives a slightly higher effective yield.

      Is FD interest taxed?

      In many countries, yes. Some banks deduct tax at source. Enter the rate to see the interest after tax.

      How a recurring deposit works

      With a recurring deposit, you pay a fixed amount into the account every month for the tenure. Each deposit earns interest from the month it’s made until maturity, compounded at the bank’s frequency, so earlier deposits earn more than later ones.

      What return should I use?

      What is CAGR?

      CAGR is the steady yearly growth rate that would take a starting value to a final value over a number of years. Real investments rarely grow evenly, but CAGR smooths out the ups and downs so different investments and time periods can be compared fairly.

      CAGR = (Final value ÷ Starting value)1/years − 1
      How is CAGR different from absolute return?

      Absolute return is the total percentage gain, regardless of time. CAGR spreads that gain over the years, so 100% over 10 years is about 7.2% a year, while 100% over 5 years is about 14.9% a year.

      Does CAGR include money added along the way?

      No. CAGR assumes a single starting amount. For regular contributions, the SIP calculator or an XIRR calculation is more accurate.

      ROI vs annualized return

      Total ROI shows the overall gain. The annualized return spreads it over the years held, which is the fairer way to compare.

      How ROI is worked out

      ROI = (Final value + income − amount invested − costs) ÷ (amount invested + costs)Annualized ROI = (1 + ROI)1/years − 1

      Total ROI tells you how much you made overall. Because it ignores time, an investment that doubled in 10 years shows the same ROI as one that doubled in 2. The annualized return fixes that, so always compare investments on an annualized basis.

      What should I include as costs?

      Include purchase and sale fees, commissions, taxes paid and any running costs such as maintenance on a property.

      What counts as income?

      Dividends, interest, rent or any cash the investment paid you while you held it.

      What is dividend yield?

      Dividend yield is the yearly dividend a company pays per share, as a percentage of the share price. It shows how much income you get for each unit of money invested, before any change in the share price.

      Dividend yield = Annual dividend per share ÷ Share price × 100

      Yield on cost

      Yield on cost compares today’s dividend with the price you originally paid. If a company keeps raising its dividend, your yield on cost can grow well above the starting yield.

      Is a high dividend yield always good?

      Not necessarily. A very high yield can mean the share price has fallen because investors expect the dividend to be cut. Check that the company can afford its dividend.

      Are dividends taxed?

      In many countries, yes. Tax rules vary, so check how dividends are taxed where you live.

      How profit and loss are worked out

      Break-even price

      The break-even price is the sell price at which you’d get back exactly what you paid, including fees, after counting any dividends received.

      Should fees be included?

      Yes. Commissions, exchange fees and stamp duty all reduce your profit, especially on smaller trades.

      How is tax worked out here?

      The tax rate is applied to the profit only when there’s a profit. Real tax rules vary by country and holding period.

      What inflation does to money

      Inflation is the general rise in prices over time. When prices rise, each unit of money buys less, so the same amount of money has less purchasing power in the future.

      Future cost = Amount × (1 + inflation)yearsBuying power = Amount ÷ (1 + inflation)years

      Beating inflation

      To grow your wealth in real terms, your savings or investments need to earn more than the inflation rate. The real return is roughly your return minus inflation.

      What inflation rate should I use?

      Many central banks aim for about 2% a year, but actual inflation varies by country and over time. Use your country’s recent average or an estimate for the future.

      What is a real return?

      The real return is what your money earns after allowing for inflation. Earning 5% when inflation is 3% gives a real return of about 1.9%.

      What is the Rule of 72?

      The Rule of 72 is a quick way to estimate how long an investment takes to double: divide 72 by the yearly return. At 8%, money doubles in about 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years. It also works the other way: to double in 6 years, you need about 72 ÷ 6 = 12% a year.

      Years to double ≈ 72 ÷ rateThe exact answer is ln(2) ÷ ln(1 + rate). The Rule of 72 is most accurate for rates between about 6% and 10%.
      Why 72?

      72 is close to the exact value from the maths (about 69.3 for continuous growth) and is divisible by many numbers, which makes mental arithmetic easy.

      Does it work for inflation and debt?

      Yes. At 6% inflation, prices double in about 12 years. A debt growing at 18% doubles in about 4 years if nothing is paid.

      How FIRE works

      Your FIRE number is the amount you need invested so that withdrawing a small, safe percentage each year covers your spending. With the common 4% rule, that’s 25 times your yearly spending. The higher your savings rate, the faster you get there, because you save more and need less.

      FIRE number = Yearly spending ÷ Safe withdrawal rateThe projection uses your return minus inflation, so all figures are in today’s money.
      Is 4% really safe?

      It comes from studies of past market returns over 30-year retirements. For longer early retirements, many people use 3 to 3.5% for extra safety.

      What are lean and fat FIRE?

      Lean FIRE means a frugal lifestyle with a smaller target. Fat FIRE means a more comfortable lifestyle and a bigger target.

      How workplace retirement funds work

      Each month, you and your employer put a percentage of your salary into the fund, and the balance earns interest or investment returns. Because contributions rise with your salary and the growth compounds, the balance can become large by retirement.

      About the schemes

      EPF Sri Lanka: employees typically contribute 8% and employers 12% of earnings, and employers also pay 3% into the separate ETF, which isn’t included here. EPF India: employees contribute 12% of basic pay, and of the employer’s 12%, 3.67% goes to EPF while 8.33% goes to the pension scheme (EPS). 401(k): you choose your contribution, employers often match part of it, and there’s a yearly contribution limit set by the IRS.

      Are the rates up to date?

      The preset rates are typical figures and can change. Interest rates and contribution limits are set each year, so check the current figures for your scheme and edit the fields.

      Does it include tax?

      No. Tax rules on contributions and withdrawals vary by country and scheme.

      How an annuity works

      An annuity turns a lump sum into a stream of regular payments. The money still invested keeps earning interest, so you receive more in total than you put in. When payments rise each year, the starting payment is lower, but it keeps pace with rising prices.

      Payment = PV × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)−n)PV is the lump sum, r the interest rate per period, and n the number of payments. Payments at the start of each period are divided by (1 + r).
      Is this the same as buying an annuity from an insurer?

      Not exactly. Insurers price lifetime annuities using life expectancy and their own rates. This calculator shows a fixed-term payout at a chosen rate.

      What is net worth?

      Net worth is everything you own minus everything you owe. It’s the clearest single number for your financial position, and watching it grow over time is a good sign your plan is working.

      Net worth = Total assets − Total liabilities

      Debt-to-asset ratio

      This is the share of your assets that is funded by debt. Lower is safer: under about 50% is usually seen as healthy, and it naturally falls as you pay down loans and build savings.

      What value should I use for my home and car?

      Use a realistic amount you could sell them for today, not what you paid.

      Is negative net worth bad?

      It’s common early in life, especially with student loans or a new mortgage. What matters most is that it’s rising over time.

      Why you need an emergency fund

      An emergency fund is cash set aside for the unexpected: a job loss, a medical bill, an urgent repair. It keeps you from relying on credit cards or loans when something goes wrong.

      How much is enough?

      A common guideline is three to six months of essential expenses. Aim for more if your income is irregular, others depend on you, or your household relies on one income. Keep it somewhere safe and easy to reach, such as a savings account.

      What counts as essential?

      Housing, utilities, food, transport, insurance and minimum debt payments: the costs you’d still have to pay if your income stopped.

      Should I invest my emergency fund?

      Usually not. It needs to be available quickly and shouldn’t fall in value when you need it.

      How income tax works

      Most countries use progressive tax: income is split into bands, and each band is taxed at its own rate. Your marginal rate is the rate on your next unit of income, while your effective rate is total tax divided by income, which is always lower.

      What’s included

      Sri Lanka: personal relief and slabs for 2026/27, plus the Budget 2027 proposal for 2027/28. India: new and old regimes for FY 2026-27, with standard deduction, Section 87A rebate, surcharge and 4% cess. United States: 2026 federal brackets and standard deduction, plus an optional flat state rate. United Kingdom: 2026/27 rates for England, Wales and Northern Ireland, including the personal allowance taper above £100,000. Scotland has different rates.

      Is this exact?

      It’s an estimate for typical cases. It doesn’t cover every allowance, credit or special rule, such as US tax credits, India’s surcharge marginal relief, or Scottish rates. Check with your tax authority or an adviser.

      How up to date are the rates?

      Rates were checked in November 2026. Tax rules change with each budget, so confirm the figures for the year you’re filing.

      Your take-home pay is what’s left after income tax, social security and any pension or retirement contributions are taken from your gross salary. Some deductions, such as pension contributions through salary sacrifice in the UK or a traditional 401(k) in the US, reduce your taxable income.

      What’s included

      Sri Lanka: APIT and EPF (8% employee, with 12% EPF and 3% ETF from the employer). India: income tax, EPF on basic pay and optional professional tax. United States: federal tax, Social Security and Medicare (FICA), 401(k) and an optional state rate. United Kingdom: income tax and employee National Insurance, with optional pension through salary sacrifice.

      Why is my payslip different?

      Employers may calculate tax each pay period, use tax codes, include benefits or bonuses, or deduct items not covered here, such as student loans or health insurance.

      How the conversion works

      Yearly salary = Hourly rate × Hours per week × Paid weeks per yearOvertime adds Overtime hours × Hourly rate × Overtime multiplier for each paid week.

      A full-time job of 40 hours a week for 52 weeks is 2,080 hours a year. If you don’t get paid holidays, reduce the paid weeks to match the weeks you actually work.

      Which is better, hourly or salaried?

      Hourly work pays for every hour, including overtime. Salaried roles usually include paid leave and benefits. Compare total yearly pay and benefits, not just the headline rate.

      Adding and removing tax

      Price with tax = Price × (1 + rate)Tax included in a price = Price with tax × rate ÷ (1 + rate)

      To remove tax, don’t just subtract the rate from the total: at 20%, a price of 120 includes 20 of tax, not 24.

      About the rates

      Sri Lanka: VAT is 18%, and financial services are taxed at 20.5% from July 2026. India: GST has 5% and 18% main rates, 40% on luxury and sin goods, and 3% on gold. Within a state it’s split equally into CGST and SGST, and between states it’s charged as IGST. UK: 20% standard, 5% reduced and 0%. US: there’s no federal sales tax, so enter your combined state and local rate.

      Which rate applies to my product?

      Rates depend on the exact product or service, and some items are exempt. Check your tax authority’s guidance for your goods.

      What is capital gains tax?

      Capital gains tax is charged on the profit when you sell an investment for more than you paid. The gain is the sale price minus the purchase price and costs such as brokerage, stamp duty and legal fees.

      What’s included

      United States: 2026 long-term rates of 0%, 15% and 20% stacked on your taxable income, short-term gains at income tax rates, and the optional 3.8% net investment income tax. United Kingdom: 18% and 24% rates with the £3,000 annual exemption. India: listed equity at 20% short-term and 12.5% long-term above ₹1.25 lakh, other assets at 12.5% long-term, plus 4% cess. Sri Lanka: 15% for individuals from June 2026, with the small-gain exemption.

      Can losses reduce my tax?

      Usually yes. Losses can often be set against gains in the same year and sometimes carried forward. Rules vary by country.

      How gratuity is calculated

      In India, gratuity is 15 days’ wages for each completed year of service, using a 26-day month: last wages × 15 × years ÷ 26. A final part year of more than six months counts as a full year. Permanent employees qualify after five years, and fixed-term employees after one year under the labour codes in force from 21 November 2025. Wages are basic pay plus dearness allowance, and must be at least 50% of total pay. Up to ₹20 lakh is tax-free for private sector employees.

      For Indian employers not covered by the gratuity law, gratuity is half a month’s average salary for each completed year of service: average salary of the last 10 months × 15 × completed years ÷ 30. Part years aren’t rounded up. Up to ₹20 lakh is tax-free.

      In Sri Lanka, the Payment of Gratuity Act gives half a month’s salary for each completed year of service, based on your last month’s salary. You qualify after five years of continuous service with an employer that has 15 or more workers.

      In the UAE, end-of-service gratuity is 21 days’ basic pay for each of the first five years and 30 days’ basic pay for each year after that, with part years counted pro rata. A day’s pay is monthly basic pay ÷ 30. You need at least one year of service, and the total is capped at two years’ pay.

      Enter the number of days’ pay given for each year of service, the number of days used for a month, and the minimum service needed. Gratuity = monthly salary × days per year ÷ days in a month × completed years.

      Do I get gratuity if I resign before five years?

      In India, permanent employees generally need five years, except on death or disablement. Fixed-term employees qualify after one year.

      Is gratuity taxed?

      For private sector employees, up to ₹20 lakh over your whole career is tax-free. Anything above that is added to your taxable income.

      Do I get gratuity if I resign before five years?

      Generally no. The Act requires at least five years of continuous service with the same employer.

      Does resigning reduce UAE gratuity?

      Under the current labour law, the gratuity formula is the same whether you resign or your employer ends the contract, once you’ve completed at least one year. Check your contract and any free zone rules.

      Where do I find my rules?

      Check your employment contract and your country’s labour law or labour department guidance.

      Percentage formulas

      X% of Y = Y × X ÷ 100X as a % of Y = X ÷ Y × 100 · % change = (New − Old) ÷ Old × 100 · Original before an X% increase = Final ÷ (1 + X ÷ 100)

      Percent vs percentage points

      If an interest rate goes from 4% to 5%, it rose by 1 percentage point, but by 25 percent. The percentage change calculator shows the percent change.

      Why can’t I reverse a percentage by subtracting it?

      A 20% rise followed by a 20% fall doesn’t get you back to the start: 100 becomes 120, then 96. To undo an increase, divide by (1 + the rate) instead.

      The 50/30/20 rule

      Spend about 50% of your take-home pay on needs (housing, food, utilities, transport, insurance and minimum debt payments), 30% on wants (eating out, entertainment, shopping, holidays), and put 20% towards savings and paying off debt faster. It’s a starting point: adjust the split if your rent is high or you’re saving for a big goal.

      What if my needs are more than 50%?

      That’s common where housing is expensive. Try to keep wants lower and protect at least some savings, even if it’s 10% to start.

      Three margins

      Gross margin = (Revenue − Cost of goods sold) ÷ RevenueOperating margin = Operating profit ÷ Revenue · Net margin = Net profit ÷ Revenue

      Gross margin shows how much each sale leaves to cover your running costs. Operating margin shows how efficiently the business runs. Net margin is what you keep after everything, including interest and tax.

      What is a good profit margin?

      It depends heavily on the industry. Retail and food often run on low net margins, while software and services can be much higher. Compare yourself with businesses like yours.

      Markup vs margin

      Markup = Profit ÷ Cost · Margin = Profit ÷ PriceMargin = Markup ÷ (1 + Markup) · Markup = Margin ÷ (1 − Margin)

      Both use the same profit, but markup compares it with your cost and margin with your selling price. Pricing with a markup when you meant a margin leaves you with less profit than planned.

      Runway and burn rate

      Runway = Cash ÷ Net monthly burnNet burn = Expenses − Revenue

      A business is “default alive” if, at current growth rates, revenue catches up with expenses before the cash runs out. Many founders aim to keep at least 12 to 18 months of runway.

      Questions

      Common questions

      How much does a dashboard cost?

      Every project is quoted after a short conversation, based on how many data sources, reports and updates you need. Smaller dashboards can be fixed-price, and you’ll know the cost before any work starts.

      Is my business data kept confidential?

      Yes. Your data is used only for your project, isn’t shared with anyone, and can be deleted when the work is done. We’re happy to sign a confidentiality agreement.

      What data do you need from us?

      Usually exports you already have: sales, costs, loans or accounts by month, product or branch, in Excel or CSV. We’ll tell you exactly what’s needed after the first conversation.

      Can the dashboard update itself?

      Yes, where your systems allow it. Many clients paste in a new monthly export and everything refreshes. Live connections are possible with tools such as Power BI and Google Sheets.

      Do you work with businesses outside Sri Lanka?

      Yes. We work by email and video call with businesses in any country, in any currency.

      Privacy policy

      Effective date: 22 November 2026 · Website: fincalglobal.com

      This privacy policy explains how FinCalGlobal (“we”, “us”, “our”) handles information when you use fincalglobal.com and its calculators (the “website”). We’ve written it in plain language. If anything is unclear, contact us at support@fincalglobal.com.

      In short: the numbers you type into our calculators stay in your browser. We don’t ask you to create an account, and we don’t sell your personal information.

      1. Who we are

      FinCalGlobal provides free online financial calculators for loans, savings, retirement, tax, everyday money and business, and offers custom calculation and data analysis services to businesses. We are responsible for the personal information described in this policy.

      2. Information you enter in calculators

      Our calculators run in your web browser. Amounts, rates, dates, names of debts or investments and other details you type in are processed on your device to show your results. We do not send these inputs to our servers, and we do not store them. When you close or refresh the page, your entries are cleared.

      When you use Download PDF, the file is created in your browser and saved to your device. We don’t receive a copy.

      3. Information collected automatically

      Like most websites, the servers that host and deliver our pages, and the third-party services listed below, may automatically receive technical information when you visit, such as your IP address, browser type, device type, operating system, referring page, the pages you view and the date and time of your visit. This is used to deliver the website, keep it secure and understand how it’s used.

      4. Cookies and similar technologies

      The calculators themselves don’t need cookies to work. If we use analytics or advertising services, they may set cookies or use similar technologies to measure visits, limit how often you see an ad, and show ads that are more relevant to you. Where the law requires it, for example in the European Economic Area and the United Kingdom, we’ll ask for your consent before non-essential cookies are used, and you can change your choice at any time.

      You can also block or delete cookies in your browser settings. Blocking cookies won’t stop the calculators from working.

      5. Advertising and affiliate links

      To keep FinCalGlobal free, we may show advertising from third-party networks such as Google AdSense. These providers may use cookies to show ads based on your visits to this and other websites. Google’s use of advertising cookies lets it and its partners show ads based on your visits to sites on the internet. You can opt out of personalised advertising through Google Ads Settings or www.aboutads.info.

      Some pages may include affiliate links to financial products or services. If you click one and sign up or buy, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. The partner may use cookies to record that you came from our website. Affiliate partners don’t receive your calculator inputs.

      6. Third-party services we use

      7. Emails you send us

      If you email us, for example about our custom calculator or data analysis services, we receive your email address, your name if you include it, and anything you write. We use this only to reply and, if you ask us to, to provide our services.

      8. How we use information

      • To provide, maintain and improve the website and calculators.
      • To keep the website secure and prevent misuse.
      • To understand which calculators are useful, using aggregated statistics.
      • To show advertising that keeps the website free.
      • To respond to your messages and provide services you request.
      • To meet legal obligations.

      9. Legal bases (EU and UK)

      If you’re in the European Economic Area or the United Kingdom, we rely on our legitimate interests to run and secure the website, your consent for non-essential cookies and personalised advertising, and steps you ask us to take, or our legitimate interests, when we reply to your emails.

      10. Sharing and selling

      We don’t sell your personal information, and we don’t share it for money. We share information only with the service providers described above, when the law requires it, or to protect our rights and the safety of our users. If you’re in California, you can opt out of the use of cookies for cross-context behavioural advertising through the choices described in sections 4 and 5.

      11. Data retention

      Calculator inputs aren’t stored. Emails are kept for as long as needed to deal with your enquiry and any services that follow, and then deleted unless we need to keep them for legal reasons. Third-party providers keep data according to their own policies.

      12. International transfers

      FinCalGlobal is used worldwide, and the services we rely on may process information in countries other than yours, including the United States. Where required, these transfers are protected by appropriate safeguards, such as standard contractual clauses.

      13. Your rights

      Depending on where you live, including under the GDPR in the EU, the UK GDPR, California law, India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act and Sri Lanka’s Personal Data Protection Act, you may have the right to:

      • ask what personal information we hold about you and get a copy;
      • ask us to correct or delete it;
      • object to or restrict how we use it;
      • withdraw consent at any time, without affecting earlier use;
      • complain to your local data protection authority.

      To use any of these rights, email support@fincalglobal.com. We may need to confirm your identity before we act on a request.

      14. Children’s privacy

      FinCalGlobal is meant for adults and isn’t directed at children under 16. We don’t knowingly collect personal information from children. If you believe a child has sent us personal information, contact us and we’ll delete it.

      15. Security

      We use reasonable measures to protect the website, including secure HTTPS connections. Because calculator inputs stay in your browser, they aren’t exposed to our servers. No method of transmission over the internet is completely secure, however.

      16. Changes to this policy

      We may update this policy from time to time, for example when we add new services. We’ll post the new version on this page and change the effective date at the top.

      About personal loans

      A personal loan is repaid in equal monthly installments at a fixed rate, so it works exactly like the EMI calculator above. Enter your loan offer to see the real cost.

      What it is

      An unsecured loan from a bank or finance company that you can use for almost anything, such as consolidating debt, home improvements, medical bills, travel or a wedding. No property or vehicle is pledged as security.

      Typical terms

      • Terms are usually 1 to 5 years, sometimes up to 7.
      • Rates are higher than on secured loans like mortgages, because there is no collateral.
      • Your rate depends mainly on your credit score, income and existing debts.

      Costs to watch

      • Processing or arrangement fees, often a percentage of the loan.
      • Compare offers by APR, which includes fees, not just the interest rate.
      • Early repayment (foreclosure) charges and late payment fees.
      • A shorter term means a higher EMI but less total interest.

      What is an EMI?

      An EMI (equated monthly installment) is the fixed amount you pay your lender every month until the loan is cleared. Each payment covers that month’s interest first, and the rest reduces the amount you owe. Early on, most of your EMI is interest. As the balance falls, more of each payment goes toward the principal.

      How the EMI is calculated

      EMI = P × r × (1 + r)n ÷ ((1 + r)n − 1) P is the loan amount, r is the monthly interest rate (annual rate ÷ 12 ÷ 100), and n is the number of monthly payments.

      For example, a loan of 1,000,000 at 10% a year for 5 years has r = 0.008333 and n = 60. That gives an EMI of about 21,247. Over 60 months you pay about 1,274,823 in total, so the interest cost is roughly 274,823.

      How to lower your total interest

      Three things change what a loan costs you: the rate, the term, and how fast you repay. A shorter term raises the EMI but cuts total interest sharply. Even a small extra payment each month goes straight to the principal, which shortens the loan and reduces every future interest charge. Try it with the extra payment slider above.

      Common questions

      Does a longer loan term save me money?

      No. A longer term lowers your monthly payment, but you pay interest for more months, so the total cost goes up. Compare the total interest figure for a few different terms before you choose.

      Is this the exact EMI my bank will charge?

      It’s a close estimate. Banks may add processing fees, insurance, or round differently, and some calculate interest daily. Check the final figure on your loan offer.

      What happens to my EMI with a floating rate?

      When a floating rate changes, the lender either changes your EMI or keeps it the same and changes the number of payments. Use this calculator with the new rate to see the effect.

      Should I prepay my loan or invest the money?

      Prepaying gives you a guaranteed return equal to your loan’s interest rate. If you can’t reliably earn more than that after tax elsewhere, prepaying is often the better choice. Check whether your lender charges a prepayment penalty first.

      Can I use this for home, car, and personal loans?

      Yes. Any loan with a fixed rate and equal monthly payments uses the same formula, whether it’s a mortgage, car loan, personal loan, or education loan.
